catholic.contraception:
The Catholic Church teaches that marriage and sexual intercourse have two purposes that belong together: the union of husband and wife and the openness to new life. On this basis it holds that artificial contraception is morally wrong, since it separates these two purposes. This was restated in the encyclical Humanae Vitae in 1968.

The Church permits married couples to use natural family planning, which relies on the woman's periods of fertility, for serious reasons, and asks couples to be generous in welcoming children. Many Catholics do not follow this teaching in practice, and it is widely discussed. Most Protestant churches accept the use of contraception in marriage, as a matter for the couple's conscience. A Protestant reader should note that the Catholic teaching is based on a particular understanding of the meaning of the marital act, and not just on concern about abortion.
ortho.contraception:
The Eastern Orthodox Church has no single, detailed teaching on contraception that applies to all its churches. Its tradition honors marriage as a way of holiness in which the couple is open to having children, and it warns against a selfish attitude to procreation. It firmly rejects any method that causes an abortion.

Beyond that, Orthodox churches and pastors differ. Some are stricter and discourage contraception, while others accept the use of non-abortifacient methods by married couples for good reasons, guided by their spiritual father and the responsibility of the couple before God. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox approach is generally pastoral rather than legal, and, unlike the Catholic Church, does not state a single rule for all cases.
baptist.deacons:
In Baptist churches, deacons are lay leaders elected by the congregation to serve the church, following the appointment of the seven in the sixth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles and the qualifications listed in the First Letter to Timothy. Their traditional role is to care for the needs of members, assist the pastor and help with the practical work of the church.

The role varies considerably. In some Baptist churches, the deacons form a board that shares in the oversight and decision-making of the church, and in others they focus on serving. Some Baptist churches have women deacons, while others reserve the office to men. A Protestant reader should note that in Baptist practice deacons are not ordained clergy who can baptize or preside at the Lord's Supper, but are elected members with a recognized service.
catholic.deacons:
In the Catholic Church, deacons are ordained ministers, forming the first of three orders of Holy Orders, with bishops and priests. A deacon is ordained by a bishop with the laying on of hands, and is understood to serve the church in the ministry of the Word, the liturgy and charity.

Deacons may baptize, proclaim the Gospel and preach the homily, assist at Mass, witness marriages and lead funeral services, but they cannot celebrate the Mass or hear confessions. There are transitional deacons, who are on the way to becoming priests, and permanent deacons, who may be married men. Only men are ordained. A Protestant reader accustomed to deacons as lay members of the congregation who serve the church will find that in Catholic usage the deacon is an ordained cleric.
lds.deacons:
In the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, deacon is an office in the Aaronic Priesthood, and it is held by boys of about twelve and thirteen years of age. Their duties include passing the sacrament, the church's version of communion, to the congregation, collecting fast offerings and helping the bishop with practical tasks.

Latter-day Saints understand the priesthood as authority from God which is given to worthy male members, beginning at a young age, and they see the office of deacon as a first step in a lifetime of service. A Protestant reader, who will think of a deacon as an adult who serves as a lay leader, should note that in this church the same word describes a young person in the first office of a priesthood held by all worthy males.
ortho.deacons:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, the deacon is an ordained member of the clergy, ranking below the priest, and is ordained by a bishop. The deacon assists in the Divine Liturgy by leading the litanies, reading the Gospel and helping the priest with the sacred vessels, and in many places also carries out charitable work.

Deacons may be married, provided they marry before ordination. Some churches have permanent deacons, while in others the office is mainly a step toward the priesthood. The church has also had other minor orders, such as readers and subdeacons. A Protestant reader who thinks of deacons as lay leaders elected by a congregation should note that in Orthodoxy the deacon is a member of the ordained clergy, whose role is closely tied to the church's liturgical life.
community_of_christ.degrees_of_glory:
The idea of degrees of glory, in which the afterlife has different kingdoms of glory, comes from a section of the Doctrine and Covenants, part of the wider Latter Day Saint scriptures. In Community of Christ it is not a central teaching, and members do not emphasize a system of ranked rewards.

The church places its weight on the grace of God, the worth of all persons and the hope of resurrection in Christ. Questions about the details of the life to come are generally left to the mercy of God, with confidence that God desires to bring people into wholeness. Members may hold varying personal views. A Protestant reader who thinks of a single heaven, and of a division between saved and lost, should note that this church does not press the more elaborate scheme found in other Latter Day Saint traditions.
lds.degrees_of_glory:
Latter-day Saints teach that after the resurrection and judgment, people will inherit one of three kingdoms of glory, called the celestial, the terrestrial and the telestial, and that these differ in glory as the sun, moon and stars do. They draw on a passage in the First Letter to the Corinthians and on a revelation recorded in the Doctrine and Covenants.

Nearly everyone is expected to inherit some kingdom of glory, even those who have lived lives that were not righteous. Only a very few would be consigned to outer darkness. The highest degree of the celestial kingdom is understood to be reserved for those who have kept the covenants made in the temple. A Protestant reader who thinks of a simple division between heaven and hell should note that the Latter-day Saint view has more gradations, and that the ordinary outcome is some measure of glory.
catholic.divorce:
The Catholic Church teaches that a valid sacramental marriage between baptized persons lasts until the death of one spouse, and that no civil divorce can dissolve it. This is called the indissolubility of marriage, and it rests on Jesus' teaching in the Gospels.

The Church may, however, declare an annulment, which is a finding that a supposed marriage was never valid from the beginning, for example because of a lack of true consent or a serious impediment. This is not divorce, and it is decided by a church tribunal. People who are civilly divorced may live separately, and remain in the Church, but if they remarry without an annulment they are not permitted to receive communion. Many Protestant churches allow remarriage after divorce, so a Protestant reader should note that Catholics regard the two situations differently.
lds.divorce:
Latter-day Saints teach that marriage is meant to last and, when performed in a temple, that it can continue beyond death, in what they call a sealing. Divorce is discouraged, but it is permitted, and the church does not forbid the remarriage of divorced persons.

A civil divorce does not by itself end a temple sealing. The cancellation of a sealing requires a separate church process, which is decided at the highest level of the church, and there are special rules about being sealed to a new spouse. Many Protestant churches treat divorce and remarriage as a matter of church discipline and conscience. A Protestant reader should note that for Latter-day Saints the most significant feature is the difference between a civil marriage and a temple sealing, and the way it affects a person's ordinances.
ortho.divorce:
The Eastern Orthodox Church holds that marriage is meant to be a lifelong union, reflecting Christ's relationship with the church. Yet it recognizes that human weakness and sin can destroy a marriage, and it permits divorce and, in some cases, remarriage, under the principle of economia, which means pastoral flexibility used to heal and not to weaken the teaching.

A second marriage is usually celebrated with a penitential character, and a third marriage is generally allowed only with limits, and never a fourth. Divorce is decided by the bishop, not the civil court alone. This differs from the Catholic teaching that a valid marriage cannot be dissolved. A Protestant reader will find that Orthodox practice is closer to many Protestant churches in allowing remarriage, but sets it within an ecclesial process with a penitential dimension.
catholic.ecumenical_councils:
The Catholic Church recognizes twenty-one ecumenical councils, gatherings of the bishops of the whole Church, beginning with the Council of Nicaea in 325 and continuing to the Second Vatican Council of the 1960s. The teaching of these councils on faith and morals is regarded as binding, when confirmed by the pope.

The early councils defined the Trinity and the person of Christ, and are shared with the Orthodox and most Protestants. The later ones, such as Trent and the First Vatican Council, are recognized only by Catholics. Catholics hold that the Holy Spirit guides the Church, meeting in council with the pope, to teach truth without error. A Protestant reader who accepts the first several councils and the creeds should note that Catholics hold the later councils to have equal authority, and that Protestants generally weigh all councils against Scripture.
church_of_the_east.ecumenical_councils:
The Church of the East, which includes the Assyrian Church of the East, accepts the first two ecumenical councils, held at Nicaea in 325 and at Constantinople in 381, and the Nicene Creed which came from them. It did not take part in later councils, since it was located mostly in the Persian Empire, outside the Roman Empire where those councils met.

It does not accept the Councils of Ephesus in 431 and of Chalcedon in 451, whose decisions about Christ and Mary it understands differently. The church teaches that Christ has two natures, human and divine, and it uses the title Mother of Christ for Mary. Other churches have sometimes called it Nestorian, a label the Assyrian Church rejects. A Protestant reader who accepts the early creeds and councils should note that this church holds fast to the first two but sets aside the later ones.
oriental_ortho.ecumenical_councils:
The Oriental Orthodox churches, which include the Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac, Armenian and Malankara churches, accept the first three ecumenical councils: Nicaea in 325, Constantinople in 381 and Ephesus in 431. They do not accept the Council of Chalcedon in 451, because they believe that its language about the two natures of Christ went in a direction which their teachers had not accepted.

They confess the teaching of Cyril of Alexandria, that Christ is one incarnate nature of God the Word, and for this reason they are sometimes called miaphysite. Many scholars of both sides think that the difference is largely one of wording. Official dialogues with the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches have produced joint statements. A Protestant reader who accepts Chalcedon should note that these churches share the same faith in Christ as fully God and fully man, but do not use its terms.
ortho.ecumenical_councils:
The Eastern Orthodox Church recognizes seven ecumenical councils, held between 325 and 787: Nicaea in 325, Constantinople in 381, Ephesus in 431, Chalcedon in 451, Constantinople in 553, Constantinople in 680 and 681, and Nicaea in 787. They defined the faith about the Trinity and the person of Christ, and, in the last of them, the place of icons.

Orthodox Christians believe that the Holy Spirit guided the church in these councils, and that their decisions are received by the whole church. They do not regard later Western councils as ecumenical. A Protestant reader who accepts the creeds and the first councils on the Trinity and Christ will find agreement there. The last council, which defended the veneration of icons, is the one which many Protestants do not accept, and Orthodox Christians treat it as of equal standing with the others.
catholic.ecumenism:
Since the Second Vatican Council, the Catholic Church has been officially committed to the work of Christian unity, which is called ecumenism. Its Decree on Ecumenism teaches that baptized Christians of other churches are brothers and sisters in Christ, in a real though imperfect communion with the Catholic Church. The older phrase, separated brethren, was used for this.

Catholics take part in dialogue with other churches, common prayer and shared work for justice and charity, and they pray for the visible unity of all Christians. They do not think this means setting aside doctrines the Church holds to be true. The Catholic Church is not a member of the World Council of Churches, though it cooperates with it. A Protestant reader should note that the Catholic goal is full visible unity, which it understands as unity in faith, sacraments and church governance under the pope.
evangelical.ecumenism:
Evangelicals generally value cooperation with other Christians in preaching the gospel, in evangelism, and in relief and mission work, and many take part in interchurch movements for these purposes. They believe that true believers in Christ are united in the Spirit across denominational boundaries.

At the same time, many Evangelicals are cautious about ecumenism in the institutional sense, meaning organized efforts to unite churches or councils of churches. They worry that unity may be pursued at the expense of doctrine, especially about the gospel and the authority of Scripture. For this reason they often prefer to speak of cooperation instead of ecumenism. A Protestant reader from a church involved in the institutional ecumenical movement should note that Evangelicals do seek unity, but on the basis of shared conviction about the gospel.
ortho.ecumenism:
The Eastern Orthodox Church takes part in dialogue with other Christian churches, and many Orthodox churches are members of the World Council of Churches. Orthodox Christians hold that Christian unity is a matter of the same faith and shared sacramental life, and not merely of good relations.

Because the Orthodox believe that their church has kept the fullness of the apostolic faith, they see the goal of unity as coming together in that faith, while carefully avoiding compromise. Opinions among Orthodox are divided. Some are engaged and hopeful about dialogue, and others are strongly critical of ecumenical activity, fearing that it could blur the truth. A Protestant reader will find that the Orthodox are willing to talk and to pray for unity, but are generally cautious about any agreement that would set aside doctrine.
baptist.elders:
In Baptist churches, the word elder is used in different ways. In some, especially Calvinistic Baptist churches, the church is led by a group of elders, one or more of whom are paid pastors and others of whom are chosen from the congregation. They share in teaching and oversight, and they use the New Testament's language of elders and overseers for the same office.

In many other Baptist churches the leadership consists of a pastor and a group of deacons, and the term elder is used little or not at all. In all these arrangements, Baptists teach that the local congregation holds final authority under Christ, and that its leaders serve with the congregation's consent. A Protestant reader from a Presbyterian church should note that Baptist elders belong to one autonomous local church and are not part of a larger body of elders.
lds.elders:
In the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, elder is an office in the Melchizedek Priesthood, held by adult male members, and it is also used as a title. Young men usually become elders around the age of eighteen or nineteen, and full-time male missionaries are addressed as Elder, while female missionaries are called Sister.

The church's apostles and other general leaders are also called Elder. Elders may bless the sick, confer the gift of the Holy Ghost and serve in a variety of responsibilities. A Protestant reader who knows elder as a leader who helps govern a congregation, as in Presbyterian and Reformed churches, should note that in this church it is the name of a priesthood office held by many men, and does not describe a governing board.
presbyterian.elders:
In Presbyterian churches, elders are ordained leaders who together govern the congregation. Two kinds are commonly named. Teaching elders, also called ministers of Word and Sacrament, preach, teach and administer the sacraments. Ruling elders are members chosen by the congregation to share in oversight, guarding doctrine and caring for the spiritual life of the people.

Both are ordained, and both sit together on the session that governs the local church and take part in the higher councils of the denomination. The point is that the whole church is served by shared leadership, with lay and ministerial voices in balance. Terminology and exact roles vary somewhat among Presbyterian denominations. A Protestant reader should note that in this system the elders are elected and ordained, and are accountable to the wider presbytery.
reformed.elders:
In Reformed churches, elders are the leaders who govern and care for the congregation. They are chosen from among the members and ordained, and together they oversee the doctrine and life of the church, visit and counsel members, and exercise discipline. In many Reformed churches they meet as a consistory or session, together with the pastor.

The tradition, following John Calvin, recognizes offices of pastor, teacher, elder and deacon. Pastors and teachers are responsible for the Word, elders share in rule and shepherding, and deacons care for the poor and for mercy ministries. The conviction is that Christ rules his church through Scripture and through leaders who serve together and are accountable to one another. A Protestant reader from a church led by a single pastor will note that Reformed churches emphasize shared leadership.
catholic.election:
Catholics teach that God chooses persons and peoples for a purpose of grace: Israel, the Church and individuals called in Christ. The Letter to the Ephesians speaks of believers being chosen in him before the foundation of the world, and Catholics accept that as part of the gospel.

They understand election as God's gracious call to holiness and to eternal life, and they teach that God desires the salvation of all. The Church rejects the idea that God predestines anyone to evil. Because human freedom and cooperation with grace are real, no one can be sure that he is among those finally chosen without a special revelation, and believers are told to persevere. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition will find that Catholics use the word election but do not teach that the chosen are fixed by an unconditional decree.
lds.election:
Latter-day Saints use the terms election and foreordination in ways that differ from the Reformed teaching. They believe that before the earth was created, God appointed certain people to particular roles or missions, such as prophets, and that this did not take away anyone's freedom to choose. They cite the words of God to Jeremiah, that he knew and sanctified him before birth.

They also speak of the covenant people as elect, meaning those who accept the covenants of the gospel. Latter-day Saints do not teach that God has predestined some individuals to be saved and others to be lost, and they place great emphasis on human agency. The phrase calling and election made sure is used for the promise of eternal life. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition should note that this church affirms foreordination for missions but rejects unconditional election to salvation.
reformed.election:
In Reformed teaching, the elect are those whom God has chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, as the Letter to the Ephesians says. Election is God's own free choice, not a response to human merit or foreseen faith, and it is the source of the calling, faith and perseverance of believers.

Reformed Christians are careful not to guess who the elect are. The gospel is preached to everyone, and anyone who believes may be sure that God has chosen him. Election is treated mainly as a doctrine of comfort and thanksgiving: a person's salvation depends on God and cannot fail. It is also a call to humility and to holiness, since the elect are chosen in order to be holy. Protestants in the Wesleyan and Arminian traditions understand election as conditioned on faith that God foresees, which Reformed teaching rejects.
anglican.episcopacy:
In Anglican churches a bishop is the chief pastor of a diocese. He or she teaches the faith, ordains priests and deacons, confirms, and oversees the clergy and the mission of the church in the diocese. Bishops are consecrated by other bishops, in a way that links the church to the apostolic ministry, and they are usually elected with the participation of clergy and laity.

Anglicans regard the episcopate as an ancient and valuable order which the church has kept, and which serves unity. Many Anglican provinces now have women bishops, though some provinces and members do not accept this. Anglicans differ on how essential bishops are for a church's life. A Protestant reader from a church without bishops should note that Anglican bishops govern together with synods of clergy and laity, and do not rule alone.
catholic.episcopacy:
In the Catholic Church, a bishop is the successor of the apostles, ordained to teach, to sanctify and to govern the local church, called a diocese, in communion with the pope. The bishop possesses the fullness of the priesthood, and can ordain priests and deacons.

Bishops together form a college which, with the pope as its head, has responsibility for the whole Church. Each diocesan bishop is the chief pastor and liturgical leader in his diocese. Catholics understand the office as instituted by Christ and part of the structure that keeps the Church united in faith and worship. A Protestant reader whose church is governed by congregations or elders should note that Catholics see bishops as essential to the Church's structure, not merely a form of administration.
methodist.episcopacy:
Many Methodist churches, including the United Methodist Church and the African Methodist Episcopal churches, have bishops who provide oversight. They preside over regional bodies called annual conferences, ordain clergy, and appoint pastors to their congregations, in what is called an itinerant system. They are elected by representatives of the church and consecrated for this work.

Methodists describe the office as one of service and leadership, and not as a claim to an unbroken succession of ordinations from the apostles. In the United Methodist Church a bishop is understood to be an elder who is set apart for oversight, not a separate order of ministry. A Protestant reader from a congregational church should note that Methodists combine a connectional system with bishops who share authority with elected conferences of clergy and lay members.
ortho.episcopacy:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, the bishop, in Greek episkopos, meaning overseer, is the center of the life of the local church. Each bishop leads his diocese, ordains clergy, and is the chief celebrant of the Eucharist, and is understood to stand in the place of Christ in the community.

Bishops are chosen from among the celibate clergy, and most are monks. All bishops are regarded as equal in their episcopal ministry, though some hold titles such as patriarch or metropolitan and have a role in leading a group of bishops. Decisions of doctrine are made in councils of bishops. A Protestant reader should note that Orthodox bishops are seen as successors of the apostles in an unbroken line and as guardians of the faith and unity of the church.
catholic.essence_and_energies:
Catholic theology speaks of God's divine essence, which is what God is, and which is simple and beyond all human understanding. It also teaches that God gives himself to believers through grace, and it distinguishes between the created effects of grace in the soul, called created grace, and the indwelling of God himself.

Catholic teachers say that sanctifying grace is a real gift that makes a person share in the divine life, while the persons of the Trinity dwell in the soul of the believer. They have not adopted the Eastern Orthodox teaching that there is a real distinction in God between his essence and his energies. Some Catholic theologians see it as compatible, and others as unnecessary. Protestants seldom use this vocabulary, so a Protestant reader can see it as a way of explaining how God, who is beyond us, can give himself to us.
oriental_ortho.essence_and_energies:
The Oriental Orthodox churches generally speak of the divine nature, which is beyond all human understanding, and of God's operations, the ways in which he acts and makes himself known. They hold that human beings can truly share in God's life through Christ and the Holy Spirit, and use the language of deification in the tradition of the early Fathers.

They do not usually use the technical vocabulary of essence and energies associated with the Eastern Orthodox teacher Gregory Palamas, since it was developed in a different setting. Their teaching about God's transcendence and about our participation in him is often close to it in meaning. A Protestant reader who does not use this vocabulary should note that the concern behind it is to say both that God is beyond knowing and that he truly gives himself to those who believe.
ortho.essence_and_energies:
Eastern Orthodox theology distinguishes between God's essence and his energies. God's essence, what he is in himself, is beyond all knowledge and cannot be shared. His energies are God himself in action, uncreated and eternal, through which he creates, sustains and saves, and in which human beings can truly participate.

This teaching is associated with Gregory Palamas in the fourteenth century. It is used to explain how people can be united with God, a process the Orthodox call theosis, without becoming God in essence. The light that the disciples saw at the Transfiguration of Christ is called the uncreated light, an energy of God. Protestants rarely use this vocabulary, so a Protestant reader should note that it is an attempt to say that grace is not merely a gift from God but the presence of God himself.
catholic.eucharistic_sacrifice:
Catholics teach that the Mass is a sacrifice. They do not mean that Christ is sacrificed again or that a new sacrifice is added to the cross. They teach that the one sacrifice of Christ on Calvary is made present in the Mass in a sacramental way, so that the Church can offer it to the Father and share in its fruits.

The priest acts in the person of Christ, and the faithful join their own prayers and lives to the offering. The Council of Trent affirmed that the Mass is a true sacrifice, of the same nature as Calvary but offered in an unbloody manner. Protestants often object that the Letter to the Hebrews says Christ was offered once for all. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics agree with this, and say the Mass is the same offering made present, not a repetition.
lutheran.eucharistic_sacrifice:
Lutherans teach that the Lord's Supper is a gift that God gives to us, and not a sacrifice which the church offers to God to obtain forgiveness. Christ offered himself once for all on the cross, and nothing can be added to it. The Supper delivers the benefits of that sacrifice to those who receive it.

Lutherans do speak of a sacrifice of praise: the church responds to the gift with thanksgiving, prayer and lives offered to God. In this sense worship includes sacrifice, but as a response and not as an attempt to earn favor. This is one of the ways Lutherans distinguish their understanding from the Catholic teaching of the Mass as a sacrifice. A Protestant reader will find that Lutherans agree with other Protestants that Christ's sacrifice is complete, while holding that the Supper is more than a bare memorial.
ortho.eucharistic_sacrifice:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Divine Liturgy is described as a bloodless sacrifice: the offering of bread and wine, with thanksgiving, which by the Holy Spirit become the body and blood of Christ. The church offers the gifts, in words of the liturgy, Thine own of Thine own, and remembers the sacrifice of Christ on the cross.

The Orthodox do not teach that the sacrifice of Christ is repeated, since it was made once. The liturgy makes it present and lets the faithful take part in it, and in the heavenly worship of the angels. The emphasis falls on thanksgiving, which is the meaning of the word Eucharist. A Protestant reader who thinks of the Lord's Supper as a memorial should note that the Orthodox hold that it is a real participation in Christ's sacrifice and in his risen life.
catholic.faith_and_works:
Catholics teach that salvation is a gift of God's grace, which no one can earn, and that faith is the beginning of justification. They also speak of faith working through love, using the words of the apostle Paul in the Letter to the Galatians, meaning that living faith shows itself in good works done in charity and by God's grace.

The Council of Trent taught that the works of a person before justification cannot merit it, but that, once justified, a believer cooperates with grace, and good works increase grace. In 1999, the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation issued a Joint Declaration stating agreement on basic truths about justification. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics do not teach that people are saved by works apart from grace, but that grace makes works possible and that they belong to the life of faith.
churches_of_christ.faith_and_works:
Members of Churches of Christ teach that salvation is by God's grace and cannot be earned. They also speak of obedient faith: a faith that responds to God by repenting, confessing Jesus as Lord and being baptized. These steps are not understood as payments or good works that earn salvation, but as the way a believer accepts the gift.

Because of this, Churches of Christ are careful to say that they do not teach salvation by works. Baptism in particular is regarded as an act of faith in which God works, and not as a human accomplishment. A Protestant reader from a church that teaches faith alone should note that Churches of Christ agree that no one earns salvation, but differ in holding that faith is completed by these responses, especially baptism, so that it is not merely an inward trust.
lds.faith_and_works:
Latter-day Saints teach that salvation comes through the grace of Jesus Christ, and they also teach that faith must be shown in works. A passage in the Book of Mormon, that it is by grace that we are saved after all we can do, is often quoted. They understand it to mean that grace makes up for what people cannot do themselves, and not that works come first.

They distinguish between two things. Resurrection and immortality come to everyone as a free gift through Christ, regardless of works. Exaltation, the fullest life with God, is available on condition of faith, repentance, baptism, temple covenants and enduring to the end. A Protestant reader who holds to faith alone should note that Latter-day Saints reject the idea that people earn salvation, but regard obedience to God's commands and covenants as part of accepting it.
ortho.faith_and_works:
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not divide faith and works into rival ways of being saved. It teaches that salvation is entirely a gift of God's grace, and that it is received and lived out through a person's free cooperation with that grace. This cooperation is called synergy, which means working together.

Faith is a living trust in Christ, and it shows itself in prayer, repentance, love of neighbor and the sacramental life. The Orthodox cite the Letter of James, that faith without works is dead, but they do not think that works earn salvation. God always begins, and the person responds. A Protestant reader accustomed to the phrase faith alone should note that the Orthodox do not use it, because they see salvation less as a legal verdict received at one moment and more as a lifelong healing and growth in union with God.
catholic.fasting:
Catholics practice fasting as a form of penance, prayer and self-discipline. The Church asks those between eighteen and fifty-nine to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, which means taking only one full meal and two smaller ones. Catholics aged fourteen and over are also asked to abstain from meat on those days and on the Fridays of Lent.

In many countries Catholics are asked to keep some form of penance on the other Fridays of the year. There is also the Eucharistic fast, of one hour before receiving communion. Catholics see fasting as a way of uniting oneself with Christ's suffering, of growing in self-control and of helping the poor. Many Protestants also fast, for prayer or repentance, but in the Catholic Church it is tied to the church's calendar and to specific rules.
lds.fasting:
Latter-day Saints keep a monthly fast on Fast Sunday, usually the first Sunday of the month. Members go without food and drink for two consecutive meals, usually about twenty-four hours, and spend the time in prayer. They also give a fast offering, at least the amount they would have spent on the meals, which the church uses to help the poor and needy.

On Fast Sunday, the main service is a testimony meeting, in which members of the congregation come forward to share their faith and experiences. Latter-day Saints may also fast at other times for specific purposes, such as seeking guidance or praying for the sick. A Protestant reader who knows fasting as a personal spiritual practice will note that here it is a regular, church-wide observance which combines prayer with care for the poor.
oriental_ortho.fasting:
The Oriental Orthodox churches keep fasting seriously as part of Christian life. The Coptic and Ethiopian churches in particular have many fasting days in the year, including most Wednesdays and Fridays, a long fast before Easter, and other seasonal fasts before feasts. Fasting usually means abstaining from meat and animal products, and often from food entirely until a certain hour of the day.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is especially known for the number of its fasting days. These churches understand fasting as a means of prayer, repentance and self-control, and as a way of sharing in Christ's own fast in the wilderness. A Protestant reader who knows fasting as an occasional personal discipline should note that in these churches it is a communal practice which shapes the whole year, and which believers keep with great earnestness.
ortho.fasting:
The Eastern Orthodox Church keeps a rhythm of fasting throughout the year. The main seasons are Great Lent before Pascha, the Nativity fast, the Apostles' fast and the Dormition fast, and most Wednesdays and Fridays are also fast days. Fasting usually means abstaining from meat, dairy products and eggs, and at certain times from wine and oil.

Orthodox teaching insists that fasting is more than diet. It is meant to go with prayer, almsgiving and repentance, and to train a person in humility and self-control, so that a fast kept with pride is worthless. The rules are adapted for the sick, the elderly, children and others, usually with the advice of a spiritual father. A Protestant reader who knows fasting as an occasional personal discipline will find that in Orthodoxy it is a shared and ordinary part of Christian life.
catholic.father:
Catholics confess God the Father as the first person of the Holy Trinity, the source and origin of all things, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. They pray to him in the Lord's Prayer, Our Father, and teach that believers, through Baptism, become his adopted children.

The Church teaches that God is not male or female, and that calling him Father is how Jesus revealed him and taught his disciples to speak. The Father eternally begets the Son and, with the Son, is the source of the Holy Spirit, in the Western understanding. A Protestant reader will find that Catholic belief about God the Father is largely the same as their own, with the difference in the doctrine of the Spirit's procession, and in Catholic devotion, which also includes prayers to Mary and the saints.
jehovahs_witnesses.father:
Jehovah's Witnesses use Jehovah as the personal name of God the Father. He is the Creator of all things and the Sovereign of the universe, and he is a loving Father to those who serve him. Jesus taught his followers to pray to the Father, and Witnesses pray to Jehovah through Jesus.

They teach that the Father is greater than the Son. The Father is the one whom Jesus calls his God, and the Father alone is Almighty. Witnesses stress the closeness of the relationship between Jehovah and those who serve him. A Protestant reader who confesses that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal persons in one God should note that Witnesses regard Jehovah the Father as the one true God, and consider the Son to be a separate, subordinate being.
lds.father:
Latter-day Saints believe in God the Father, whom they usually call Heavenly Father, and sometimes Elohim. They teach that he is a personal being with a glorified, perfected body of flesh and bone, who is the literal father of the spirits of all human beings, so that every person is his spirit child.

They distinguish him as a separate being from the Son, Jesus Christ, and from the Holy Ghost, and they use the name Elohim for the Father and Jehovah for the premortal Christ. Most Protestants hold that God is spirit and that the Father is one person in the Trinity, with the same essence as the Son. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints share the language of Father and prayer, but use it with a different understanding of God's nature and of our relationship to him.
oneness_pentecostal.father:
For Oneness Pentecostals, Father is a title of the one God, and not the name of a separate person alongside the Son. God is Father in that he is the creator and the source of all things, and Father to his people. Jesus is not another person distinct from the Father, but the same God who is Father, revealed in human flesh.

Oneness believers read passages in which Jesus speaks of the Father as referring to the deity dwelling in the human nature of Jesus. This differs from the traditional Trinitarian view that the Father and the Son are two eternally distinct persons. A Protestant reader who holds to the Trinity should note that Oneness Pentecostals also confess one God and honor the Father, but do not speak of him as one of three persons.
ortho.father:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that God the Father is the one source, or the unoriginate origin, of the Godhead. From him the Son is eternally begotten, and the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds. This is sometimes called the monarchy of the Father, and it is central to Orthodox teaching about the Trinity.

The Father is confessed as almighty maker of heaven and earth, as in the Nicene Creed, and as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Orthodox stress that the persons of the Trinity share one divine nature, and that the Father is the source of their unity. A Protestant reader will find the language of Father, Son and Holy Spirit familiar, but should note that Orthodox teaching makes the Father's role as source the starting point for understanding the Trinity.
catholic.filioque:
The Catholic Church confesses that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Latin word filioque, meaning and from the Son, was added to the Nicene Creed in the Western church during the early Middle Ages, and Catholics use it in the Creed in Latin liturgy.

Catholic theology explains that the Father and the Son are together a single source of the Spirit, and that the Father remains the origin of the Godhead. The Catholic Church holds that the phrase expresses a truth about the Trinity found in Scripture and the Fathers. Eastern Christians object both to the change in the Creed, made without an ecumenical council, and to the theology. Most Protestants inherited the Western form of the Creed and use it, so a Protestant reader should note that this is a point of division with the Orthodox.
oriental_ortho.filioque:
The Oriental Orthodox churches use the Nicene Creed without the filioque, so they confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. They did not take part in the Western church's addition of the phrase, and they generally follow the form of the Creed that was received by the early councils.

Their concern is both about the wording and about the way it might affect their understanding of the Trinity, in which the Father is the source of the divine persons. Practice has not been the same in every church and every period, but the general tradition is to keep the older form. Most Protestants use the Western form, with the added phrase, so a Protestant reader should note that these churches are with the Eastern Orthodox and against the Western additions on this point.
ortho.filioque:
The Eastern Orthodox Church rejects the addition of the filioque, the phrase and from the Son, to the Nicene Creed. The Orthodox teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, who is the one source of the Godhead, while the Son sends the Spirit in time, as the Gospel of John says.

They object to two things: that the Western church altered the Creed on its own, without an ecumenical council, and that the added phrase seems to them to put two sources in the Trinity and so to confuse the persons. It has been a long-standing point of division between East and West. Most Protestants inherited the Western text of the Creed, so a Protestant reader should note that Orthodox Christians say the older form and think it matters, though many Western Christians regard it as a minor difference in wording.
adventist.food_laws:
Many Adventists follow what they call the health message, which includes avoiding the foods that the Old Testament calls unclean, such as pork and shellfish, and many choose to be vegetarian. They understand these guidelines as principles of health that come from the Creator, and as a way of caring for the body which is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Adventists do not teach that these choices bring salvation, and they view them as a matter of stewardship and faithfulness. They read passages such as the vision of Peter in the Acts of the Apostles as being about the acceptance of Gentile people, and not as declaring all foods clean. Most other Protestants hold that all foods are clean, as taught in the Gospel of Mark and elsewhere, so a Protestant reader should note that Adventists see the dietary principles as still valid.
jehovahs_witnesses.food_laws:
Jehovah's Witnesses abstain from blood, following the commands in Genesis and Leviticus and the decree of the apostles recorded in Acts to abstain from blood. They therefore do not eat blood, and they refuse transfusions of whole blood and its principal components: red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.

Most Protestants hold that all foods are clean and that the decree in Acts was a temporary measure to help Jewish and Gentile believers eat together, so they accept blood transfusions. Witnesses hold that the command is permanent and applies to receiving blood into the body by any route, because blood represents life, which belongs to God. They accept other medical treatments, and the use of some blood fractions is left to individual conscience. A Protestant reader should note that Witnesses regard this as obedience to God and not as a refusal of medicine.
lds.food_laws:
Latter-day Saints do not follow the food laws of the Old Testament, but they keep the Word of Wisdom, a health law found in the Doctrine and Covenants, which they believe was given by revelation in the 1830s. It encourages eating grains, fruits and vegetables, and using meat sparingly, and it forbids alcohol, tobacco, and hot drinks, which are understood to mean tea and coffee.

Keeping the Word of Wisdom is a requirement for entering the temple, and it is accompanied by promises of health and wisdom. Most Protestants do not consider any foods forbidden and leave matters of diet to Christian freedom. A Protestant reader should note that for Latter-day Saints the Word of Wisdom is not about ritual cleanness, as in the Old Testament laws, but about health and self-mastery, and it is treated as a commandment from God.
messianic.food_laws:
Many Messianic Jews and other Messianic believers choose to keep kashrut, the biblical food laws as understood in Jewish tradition, such as avoiding pork and shellfish and keeping meat and dairy apart. For them it expresses Jewish identity, obedience to God's instruction and solidarity with the Jewish people.

Messianic believers generally teach that this is a matter of practice and conscience, not a requirement for salvation, and that Gentile believers are not bound to it. They read New Testament passages about food in different ways, and some congregations keep kosher strictly, others partly and others not at all. Most Protestants believe that Christ made all foods clean and eat freely. A Protestant reader should note that Messianic believers see faith in Yeshua as compatible with continued Jewish practice.
adventist.foot_washing:
Adventists practice foot washing as an ordinance of humility, alongside the Lord's Supper. It is done as part of the communion service, held usually four times a year. Members are invited to wash one another's feet, in pairs, with men and women often in separate rooms or in family groups, following the example of Jesus in the Gospel of John.

After foot washing, the congregation shares unleavened bread and unfermented grape juice. Adventists understand the foot washing as a sign of humility, of forgiveness and of readiness to serve one another, and as a preparation for the Supper. It is not regarded as saving anyone. Most other Protestants do not practice foot washing as an ordinance, so a Protestant reader should note that Adventists treat it as an act of obedience to Jesus' command.
anabaptist.foot_washing:
Some Anabaptist groups practice foot washing as an ordinance, following Jesus' washing of the disciples' feet in the Gospel of John and his instruction that they should do likewise. It is understood as a sign of humility, service and love within the community, and it often accompanies the observance of communion.

Practice differs. It is regular among the Amish and many Old Order and conservative Mennonite groups, while many mainstream Mennonite churches do it only occasionally or not at all. Where it is practiced, believers usually wash and dry one another's feet in pairs, men with men and women with women. A Protestant reader from a church that treats it as a symbolic gesture should note that for these Anabaptists it is a serious act of obedience and of reconciliation, and not only a symbol.
catholic.foot_washing:
Catholics observe the washing of feet on Holy Thursday, at the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper. The priest, following the example of Jesus in the Gospel of John, washes the feet of a number of people from the congregation, traditionally twelve men. In recent years the Church has allowed the rite to include women as well as men.

This rite, called the mandatum, is not one of the seven sacraments. It is a symbolic act which recalls Jesus' service, and the new commandment to love one another, which is the origin of the word Maundy. It is not practiced as a regular ordinance at other times. A Protestant reader from a tradition that does not wash feet will find that Catholics see it as a solemn part of the Holy Week liturgy.
oneness_pentecostal.foot_washing:
Some Oneness Pentecostal churches practice foot washing as an ordinance, following the example of Jesus in the Gospel of John, who washed his disciples' feet and told them to do the same. It is understood as an act of humility and service, and it is often performed as part of a communion service.

Practices differ among Oneness Pentecostal organizations and congregations. Some keep foot washing regularly, some occasionally, and some do not observe it as a formal ordinance. Where it is practiced, believers usually wash one another's feet in pairs. A Protestant reader from a church that does not practice it should note that it is regarded as a matter of obedience to Christ's example and not as something that saves.
catholic.free_will:
Catholics teach that human beings have free will, as part of being made in the image of God, and that they are responsible for their choices. Sin has wounded human nature and inclined it to evil, but it has not destroyed freedom. The Council of Trent condemned the idea that free will was lost by the Fall.

At the same time, Catholics hold that people need grace to turn to God and to do good, and that God's grace always comes first. A person's cooperation with grace is a free act which grace itself makes possible. This differs from the Reformed teaching that the will is in bondage to sin and is freed only by regeneration. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics stress both God's initiative and human cooperation, and that they see no contradiction in doing so.
lds.free_will:
Latter-day Saints place great weight on agency, which they usually call free agency: the God-given capacity to choose and to act, and not merely to be acted upon. They believe that agency is essential to God's plan, and that it existed before the earth was created, when a contest arose over whether to preserve it.

They teach that people are free to choose between good and evil, and are accountable for their choices, and that the opportunity to choose in a world of opposition is the purpose of mortal life. Grace supports the effort, and the Atonement makes repentance possible. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition, who holds that the human will is bound by sin, should note that Latter-day Saints believe agency is a fundamental part of human nature that has not been lost.
methodist.free_will:
Methodists believe that human beings can freely respond to God, and that they are responsible for their answer. Because of the effects of sin, this freedom does not come by nature. It is restored by God's prevenient grace, which goes before and enables every person to accept or to resist the offer of salvation.

This means that faith is a real human act, and also a gift made possible by God, so that no one can boast. It also means that God does not force anyone, and that people can refuse. Methodists distinguish their view from the Reformed teaching that God's choice alone decides, and from views in which people can save themselves. A Protestant reader should note that Methodists understand free will as grace-enabled and always dependent on God, and not as an independent power.
ortho.free_will:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that human beings have real freedom, as part of the image of God in them, and that God never forces a person's will. The Fall damaged human nature and weakened the will, but it did not remove freedom or make people incapable of responding to God.

Salvation is understood as the cooperation, or synergy, of God's grace and the human will. God takes the initiative and gives grace, and the person freely responds. The Orthodox do not teach that a person can save himself, and the initiative is always God's. A Protestant reader from the Reformed tradition, which holds that the will is enslaved to sin until God renews it, should note that the Orthodox place much more emphasis on human freedom and cooperation, and do not accept that inability is total.
reformed.free_will:
Reformed Christians teach the bondage of the will: because of sin, the human will is enslaved, so that people in their natural state freely choose according to their sinful desires and will not turn to God unless he changes them. They are still responsible for what they choose, since they choose willingly, and no one is forced to sin.

Reformed Christians use the term free agency for this: people act voluntarily, but their will is not neutral. Only when God renews the heart by his Spirit are they freed to love and follow him. This is why the tradition speaks of regeneration, the new birth, as coming before faith and enabling it. Protestants in the Wesleyan and Arminian traditions teach instead that God's prevenient grace restores the ability of every person to respond, so a Protestant reader should note that the Reformed use of free will differs from theirs.
catholic.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Catholics speak of two things which Protestants may describe by a single phrase. The first are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, named in the book of Isaiah: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. They are given to every baptized person and strengthened in Confirmation, and they help a Christian to live according to the Spirit.

The second are the charisms, special graces such as healing, prophecy, teaching or administration, which are listed in the First Letter to the Corinthians. These are given to particular members for the good of the whole Church, and the Church's pastors are responsible for discerning them. A Protestant reader who uses the phrase spiritual gifts for the second kind should note that Catholics also count the first kind, which belong to every believer.
lds.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Latter-day Saints believe that the gifts of the Spirit, such as those listed in the First Letter to the Corinthians and in the Book of Mormon, including wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment and tongues, are given to faithful members of the church today. They understand them as coming through the gift of the Holy Ghost, received after baptism.

The gifts are meant for the benefit of others and are to be used with humility and reverence, and not for display. Members are encouraged to seek them, and there are formal blessings, such as blessings for the sick, given by priesthood holders. A Protestant reader from a Pentecostal tradition should note that Latter-day Saints affirm the gifts, but their worship services are quiet, and tongues and prophecy are not a regular feature of public worship.
ortho.gifts_of_the_spirit:
The Eastern Orthodox Church affirms that the Holy Spirit gives gifts, called charismata, to the members of the Church, as described in the First Letter to the Corinthians. The Spirit is given to every Christian in Chrismation, and the gifts are understood as belonging to the life of the whole body, and as always serving love, the greatest of them.

Orthodox teaching is cautious about seeking extraordinary or ecstatic experiences, since these may be deceptive, and it places far more weight on humility, repentance and the ordinary life of prayer and the sacraments. Such gifts as healing and insight are recognized in the lives of the saints, and are treated as signs of God's grace. A Protestant reader from a Pentecostal or charismatic church should note that Orthodox Christians honor the gifts, but do not usually make them the center of church life.
pentecostal.gifts_of_the_spirit:
Pentecostals believe that the Holy Spirit still gives spiritual gifts to believers for the building up of the church. They often speak of nine gifts, following the list in the First Letter to the Corinthians: a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, different kinds of tongues, and the interpretation of tongues.

The gifts are understood as given by the Spirit as he chooses, not earned, and their purpose is to serve others and to strengthen the church. Pentecostals also teach that gifts should be exercised in an orderly manner, weighed against Scripture and used with love. Many other Protestants believe in spiritual gifts, but hold that some of the more miraculous ones have ceased, so a Protestant reader should note that Pentecostals expect all of them to operate in worship today.
catholic.glorification:
Catholics teach that the final goal of salvation is glorification: the sharing of the saved in the glory of God. At death, those who die in God's friendship, and are fully purified, see God face to face, an experience called the beatific vision. At the end of time their bodies will be raised and glorified, sharing in the risen life of Christ.

This is understood as the fulfillment of what God intended for human beings, to know and love him and to be united with him forever. It is a gift and not something earned, though it is reached by cooperating with grace. Many Protestants describe glorification as the last stage of salvation, in which believers are made perfect at Christ's return. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics stress the vision of God as the center of eternal life, and that they include the saints in heaven as part of the communion.
lds.glorification:
Latter-day Saints speak of exaltation, also called eternal life, which they understand as the highest degree of glory in the celestial kingdom, in which those who have kept their covenants live in the presence of God and continue as families forever. They teach that it is made possible by the Atonement of Jesus Christ, and requires faith, repentance, baptism, temple ordinances and enduring to the end.

Latter-day Saints also teach that human beings are children of God who can become like him, receiving all that the Father has. They see this as growth in godliness and not as equality with God the Father. Many Protestants speak of glorification as the completion of salvation in which believers are made perfect, but do not teach that people can become like God. A Protestant reader should note that the Latter-day Saint idea includes eternal progression and family relationships.
catholic.grace:
Catholics teach that grace is the free and undeserved help that God gives, by which he shares his own life with human beings. They distinguish sanctifying grace, a lasting gift received in Baptism that makes a person holy and pleasing to God, from actual grace, God's help for a particular good act or decision.

Grace is not earned. It comes from God's initiative, and it is given especially through the sacraments. Catholics stress that grace not only forgives sin but transforms a person, making him a sharer in the divine nature, in the words of the Second Letter of Peter. Protestants commonly define grace as unmerited favor, and Catholics agree that it is unmerited, but a Protestant reader should note that Catholics also speak of grace as a real gift within the soul, and not only as God's attitude toward us.
lds.grace:
Latter-day Saints teach that salvation comes through the grace of Jesus Christ, and that no one can be saved by his own works alone. They understand grace as both God's mercy, which forgives sin, and his enabling power, which helps people to change and to do what they could not do alone.

A line from the Book of Mormon, that it is by grace that we are saved after all we can do, is often misunderstood by other Christians to mean that people earn grace. Latter-day Saints explain that it means that no one can do enough alone, and that grace makes up the difference. Obedience is seen as a response to grace, and not a payment. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints share the language of grace and dependence on Christ, but include obedience and covenants as part of receiving it.
ortho.grace:
The Eastern Orthodox Church understands grace not mainly as God's favor, but as God's own life and presence, given to human beings. It is uncreated, meaning that it is God himself in action, called his energies, and is not a created thing given to us by God. Through grace human beings are healed, and drawn into union with him.

Orthodox teaching links grace with the sacraments, prayer and a life of repentance, and with a process of growth called theosis, in which the believer shares more and more in the divine life. Grace is never earned, and always precedes human effort, yet a person is called to cooperate with it. A Protestant reader who thinks of grace as unmerited favor will find that the Orthodox agree, but they emphasize that grace is God's presence that transforms, not only his forgiveness.
reformed.grace:
Reformed Christians speak of sovereign grace: salvation begins and ends with God's free favor toward sinners who deserve only judgment. Grace is not earned, and it is not merely offered and then left to depend on human response, but it is effective, accomplishing what God intends.

The Holy Spirit brings those whom God has chosen to faith in a way that overcomes their resistance, which is often called effectual or irresistible grace. Because of this, the tradition gives all the credit to God. Reformed Christians also speak of common grace, the goodness God shows to all people in providing for them and restraining evil. A Protestant reader from the Wesleyan or Arminian tradition will find that Reformed churches use the same word, but hold that grace does not depend on a person's decision to receive it.
adventist.great_apostasy:
Adventists have taught that the church fell into a period of apostasy after the time of the apostles, in which teachings and practices departed from Scripture. They interpret prophecies in the books of Daniel and Revelation as describing this period, and they often point to the shift of worship from the seventh-day Sabbath to Sunday as an example.

They understand the Adventist movement as calling people back to the faith of the Bible, and speak of a remnant who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. This does not mean that only Adventists can be saved, since they teach that God has faithful people in all churches. A Protestant reader should note that Adventists share with the Reformers the idea of a return to Scripture, and add a particular reading of prophecy and the Sabbath.
catholic.great_apostasy:
Catholics do not teach that the Church fell into a complete apostasy. They hold to the indefectibility of the Church: the belief that, because of Christ's promise that the gates of hell would not prevail against it, the Church will never lose the truth of the gospel or its holiness in its teaching and sacraments.

This does not mean that its members, or even its leaders, are free of sin, and Catholics acknowledge that there have been serious failures and periods of corruption. They hold that the Church itself has been kept from teaching error in the faith. This view differs from those of Restorationist groups, who teach that true Christianity was lost, and from some Protestants who view the medieval church as deeply corrupted. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics understand the Reformation as a rupture in the Church and not as a recovery of a lost gospel.
jehovahs_witnesses.great_apostasy:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that after the death of the apostles the Christian church gradually fell into apostasy, as the apostles themselves had warned. In their view, false teachings such as the Trinity, the immortal soul and eternal torment in hell entered the church, and true worship was lost from the earth for many centuries.

They believe that Jehovah began to restore true worship in modern times, in their understanding beginning with Bible students in the late nineteenth century, who studied the Bible and rejected teachings which they considered unbiblical. Witnesses therefore see themselves as the restored form of first-century Christianity. A Protestant reader should note that many Protestants trace their churches to the apostles by continuous history and to the Reformation as a recovery of the gospel, and not by a complete loss of true Christianity.
lds.great_apostasy:
Latter-day Saints teach that after the death of the apostles, the authority of the priesthood and much of the church's teaching was lost from the earth, in what they call the Great Apostasy. They believe that plain and precious truths and ordinances were changed, and that this condition lasted for many centuries.

They hold that the Protestant Reformers were good and inspired men who prepared the way, but that they did not restore the priesthood authority. In their account, the Restoration began in the 1820s, when God appeared to Joseph Smith and, through heavenly messengers, gave him the authority to found the church again. A Protestant reader should note that Latter-day Saints honor the Reformers but hold that the Reformation was preparatory, and that it did not restore the church.
ortho.great_apostasy:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that the Church has never lost the apostolic faith, and it rejects the idea of a total apostasy. It holds that Christ promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against the Church, and that the Holy Spirit has guarded the Church in truth throughout its history.

The Orthodox do not deny that heresies, schisms and moral failures have troubled the Church, and they believe that some groups, including in the West, have departed from the faith. They do not believe that the Church itself ceased to exist or had to be restored. A Protestant reader whose tradition speaks of a return to the Bible should note that the Orthodox believe the faith has been preserved in continuous form, in worship, councils and Fathers, and that nothing needed to be recovered from the past.
restorationist.great_apostasy:
Many Restorationists teach that after the time of the apostles the church gradually departed from the teaching and practice of the New Testament, a departure often described as the apostasy or the falling away. They point to biblical warnings about false teachers and to what they see as later additions to doctrine and worship.

Restorationists differ widely about how complete this departure was. Some, such as those in the Stone-Campbell tradition, generally hold that the church never entirely ceased to exist and needed reformation and return to the Bible. Others teach that true authority or truth was lost altogether and had to be restored by God. A Protestant reader should note that this is stronger than the Reformers' view, which was that the church needed to be reformed and not that it had been replaced.
anabaptist.head_covering:
In some Anabaptist communities, women wear a prayer covering or head covering, a small cap or scarf, as a way of following the teaching about prayer and headship in the First Letter to the Corinthians. It is understood as a sign of order in creation and of a woman's prayerful place in the church, and it is worn by many Amish and by Old Order and conservative Mennonite women, often throughout the day.

Practice varies. Hutterite women commonly wear a head scarf, while most mainstream Mennonite congregations no longer require any covering. Where it is kept, the covering is regarded as a serious matter of obedience and community identity, and its style often shows which group a woman belongs to. A Protestant reader from a church without such a practice should note that Anabaptists who do not wear one generally read the passage as reflecting the customs of its own time.
catholic.head_covering:
Traditionally, Catholic women covered their heads in church with a hat or a lace veil, called a chapel veil or mantilla, as a sign of reverence, drawing on a passage in the First Letter to the Corinthians. The 1917 Code of Canon Law required it.

The requirement was not repeated in the 1983 Code, and in most churches today it is not expected. Some women still choose to wear a veil, especially at the traditional Latin Mass, as a personal expression of humility and devotion. It is a custom and not a doctrine. A Protestant reader who knows head covering as a matter of biblical obedience, as in some Anabaptist groups, should note that in Catholic life it is now an optional devotional practice, no longer a rule.
ortho.head_covering:
In the Eastern Orthodox tradition, women have customarily covered their heads in church with a scarf, following the teaching in the First Letter to the Corinthians and the practice of the early Christians. Men uncover their heads in church.

The custom is widely kept in traditional and immigrant communities, and in some places all women wear a scarf during services. In other places, particularly in some Orthodox churches in the West, it is left to the woman's choice and many do not cover their heads. Orthodox teaching regards it as a matter of church custom and reverence rather than of doctrine. A Protestant reader should note that the practice varies among Orthodox jurisdictions, and is stronger where the local culture has preserved it.
catholic.headship:
Catholic teaching describes men and women as equal in dignity, since both are made in the image of God, and as complementary, made for each other with different gifts. It speaks of marriage as a mutual gift of self, and it interprets the apostle Paul's instructions in the Letter to the Ephesians in light of his opening words, that Christians submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.

Catholic teaching also holds that the priesthood is reserved to men, following Christ's choice of the apostles, and it teaches this as a matter of vocation, not of superiority. Popes have written about the dignity and vocation of women. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics generally use the language of complementarity rather than that of headship, and do not usually organize the discussion around male leadership in the home.
evangelical.headship:
Evangelicals hold two main views about the roles of men and women. Complementarians teach that men and women are equal in worth and dignity but have different roles, so that husbands are called to lead their families with loving, sacrificial care, and that pastoral leadership in the church is reserved to men. They rely on passages such as those in the Letter to the Ephesians and the First Letter to Timothy.

Egalitarians hold that Scripture calls for equal partnership in the home and equal opportunity for leadership in the church, and they point to passages such as the statement in the Letter to the Galatians that there is neither male nor female in Christ. Evangelical churches and organizations are divided between the two views, and it is one of the main debates within the movement. A Protestant reader should note that both sides appeal to the Bible and seek to be faithful to it.
lds.headship:
Latter-day Saints teach that in the family, the husband and wife are equal partners, and that fathers preside over their families in love and righteousness, as stated in a 1995 document called The Family: A Proclamation to the World. Mothers are described as primarily responsible for nurturing children.

The church teaches that presiding is meant to be a service, not domination, and it encourages couples to make decisions together in council. Women hold leadership positions in the church's organizations, such as the Relief Society, but priesthood office is held by men. A Protestant reader who knows the language of headship should note that Latter-day Saints speak of presiding, and that in practice the emphasis is on partnership, though the difference in roles between men and women is clear.
ortho.headship:
The Eastern Orthodox Church draws on the apostle Paul's teaching in the Letter to the Ephesians that the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the church, and it stresses that this headship is defined by Christ's self-giving love and not by domination. Husband and wife are called to submit to one another in reverence for Christ.

In the Orthodox marriage service, the couple is crowned as a sign of a shared royal priesthood in their household. The priesthood is reserved for men. Orthodox teachers and communities differ in how they speak of these matters and how they apply them in practice. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox use the language of headship, but generally do not organize the topic around debates over roles, and they place stress on marriage as a path to holiness.
catholic.heaven:
Catholics teach that heaven is the state of supreme and lasting happiness, in which the saved live in the presence of God, seeing him face to face, in what is called the beatific vision. It is understood as communion with the Holy Trinity, with the Virgin Mary, the angels and all the saints.

Those who die in God's grace but need further purification enter heaven after being purified. Catholics teach that at the end of time the bodies of the saved will be raised, and that heaven will be renewed with a new heaven and a new earth. Heaven is described as a state as much as a place. A Protestant reader will find that the Catholic belief in heaven is the same in its basic hope, and that the differences concern purification after death and the communion with the saints.
jehovahs_witnesses.heaven:
Jehovah's Witnesses believe that a limited number, 144,000, are chosen to go to heaven to reign with Christ, drawing on passages in the book of Revelation and Jesus' reference to a little flock. These are spirit-anointed Christians, and they are said to receive heavenly life after being raised from the dead.

Most Witnesses do not expect to go to heaven. Their hope is to live forever on a restored earth, and only those who have the heavenly hope share in the bread and wine at the yearly Memorial of Christ's death. Witnesses see heaven as the dwelling place of God and the angels and the place from which Christ rules. A Protestant reader who expects all believers to go to heaven should note that Witnesses hold two hopes, one heavenly for a few and one earthly for the many.
lds.heaven:
Latter-day Saints speak of heaven in a more layered way than most Protestants. They teach that after death the righteous go to a state of rest called paradise in the spirit world, and that after the resurrection and judgment people will inherit one of three kingdoms of glory. The highest of them, the celestial kingdom, is what they usually mean by heaven, where they will live in the presence of God.

They believe that the celestial kingdom is reached through faith in Christ, repentance, baptism, temple covenants and enduring to the end, and that families that have been sealed in the temple will remain together there. The lower kingdoms are also glorious. A Protestant reader who thinks of a single heaven, which all believers enter through faith, should note that the Latter-day Saint view includes several degrees of glory and a distinction between the saved and the exalted.
ortho.heaven:
In the Eastern Orthodox Church, heaven is understood mainly as the presence of God and the life of the age to come, and not chiefly as a place. The saints are already with Christ in a foretaste of that life, and the church on earth joins in worship with them and the angels in the Divine Liturgy. Paradise is often used for the state of the righteous before the general resurrection, and as the restored garden.

Orthodox teaching does not describe heaven in great detail and warns against speculation. The final hope is the resurrection of the body and life in a renewed creation, with union with God, called theosis, as its center. A Protestant reader will find the Orthodox hope familiar in its main outline, and should note that it is expressed in terms of participation in the life of God and of the communion of the church in heaven and on earth.
catholic.hell:
Catholics teach that hell is real and eternal: it is the state of definitive self-exclusion from communion with God and the blessed, to which those who die in mortal sin without repenting are consigned. The Church teaches that God does not predestine anyone to hell, and that those who go there do so by their own free choice of refusing his love.

Catholic teaching describes the chief punishment of hell as the loss of God, for whom human beings were made, and it uses the biblical images of fire to speak of its suffering. The Church has never said that any particular person is in hell, and it prays for the salvation of all. A Protestant reader will find that Catholics and most Protestants agree that hell is eternal, though Catholics also teach purgatory, a state of purification for those who die in grace but are not yet fully cleansed.
jehovahs_witnesses.hell:
Jehovah's Witnesses do not believe in a place of eternal fiery torment. They understand the words often translated as hell, Sheol and Hades, as referring to the common grave, where the dead are unconscious. Gehenna is understood as a symbol of everlasting destruction and not of torture.

They hold that eternal conscious punishment would be contrary to the love and justice of Jehovah, and that the Bible teaches that the wages of sin is death. Those who die are not suffering, and those who are destroyed will not exist again. They see the teaching of hellfire as something that has turned many people away from God. A Protestant reader who holds to eternal conscious punishment should note that Witnesses read the same passages as describing final destruction, and that some Protestants also hold this view.
lds.hell:
Latter-day Saints use the word hell in more than one way. They teach that after death, the wicked, and those who have not heard the gospel, go to a part of the spirit world called spirit prison, sometimes also called hell, where they can learn about Christ and choose to repent. It is understood as a temporary state, and not as a final sentence.

After the resurrection and judgment, almost everyone will inherit some kingdom of glory. The only ones consigned to outer darkness, the closest thing to the eternal punishment of other traditions, are those who knowingly reject the Holy Ghost after full knowledge, called sons of perdition, which is expected to be a very small number. A Protestant reader who thinks of hell as the eternal fate of all who reject Christ should note that Latter-day Saints understand judgment as much more graded and hopeful.
ortho.hell:
The Eastern Orthodox Church teaches that there is eternal punishment for those who finally reject God, but it usually explains it differently from a place of torture that God has prepared. Many Orthodox writers describe hell as the experience of God's own love and presence by those who have refused to love him. The same divine light which brings joy to the saved becomes torment to those who resist it.

The Orthodox use the word Hades for the realm of the dead before the resurrection, and the Last Judgment for the final decision. The church does not define the details, and Orthodox writers have used varied images. Some Orthodox theologians hope that all may finally be saved, while holding that this cannot be taught as a doctrine.
