A Protestant reader will notice that the emphasis falls on the state of the heart in relation to God, and less on a legal sentence.
catholic.hermeneutics:
Catholics hold that Scripture is to be interpreted within the living Tradition of the Church, and that the task of giving an authentic interpretation belongs finally to the Church's teaching office, the Magisterium, which is made up of the pope and the bishops in communion with him. It is not left to each reader to decide alone.

Catholic study of the Bible uses the tools of history and language, and it recognizes several senses of Scripture: the literal, and the spiritual senses, which are the allegorical, moral and heavenly. Catholics read each passage in the context of the whole Bible, the Church's tradition and the analogy of faith. A Protestant reader who values private judgment, and the principle that each believer may read and interpret the Bible, should note that Catholics regard the Bible as the Church's book, and not as something that stands apart from the community that gave it.
ortho.hermeneutics:
The Eastern Orthodox Church holds that Scripture is properly understood within the Church, in the light of the Holy Tradition, the teaching of the Fathers, the councils and the worship of the church. The Bible is read in the liturgy, and its meaning is shaped by the hymns, prayers and feasts.

The Orthodox look for the consensus of the Fathers, the general agreement of the church's early teachers, as a guide, and they read the Old Testament as pointing to Christ. Individuals may study the Bible, but they are advised not to interpret it in isolation from the life and faith of the church. There is no single teaching office, like the Catholic Magisterium, that gives official interpretations. A Protestant reader should note that the Orthodox value the Bible highly, and consider that it is rightly read only within the church that produced it.
reformed.hermeneutics:
Reformed interpreters hold that Scripture is its own best interpreter: the rule for understanding a difficult passage is to compare it with other parts of the Bible, letting the clearer passages shed light on the darker ones. This is called the analogy of faith, and rests on the belief that Scripture, though written by many people, has one divine author and does not contradict itself.

The Westminster Confession says that the infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is Scripture itself. Reformed readers also read the whole Bible as pointing to Christ, and pay attention to context, language and the way God's covenant unfolds. Creeds and the teachings of the church are used as aids, not as authorities above Scripture. A Protestant reader will find this familiar, since it is the principle behind much Protestant Bible study, though Reformed teaching places particular weight on the unity and consistency of the whole.
anglican.holy_orders:
Anglicans understand the ordained ministry as consisting of three orders: bishops, priests and deacons. Persons are ordained to these orders by the prayer of the church and the laying on of hands by a bishop, following the rites of the Ordinal in the Book of Common Prayer or its successors.

The church holds that God calls people to this ministry and that the church tests and affirms the call. Anglo-Catholics understand Holy Orders as a sacrament, while others regard it as an ancient order of ministry without calling it a sacrament of the gospel. Women are ordained as priests and deacons in many Anglican provinces, and as bishops in a number of them, although some provinces and members do not accept this development. A Protestant reader should note that Anglicans keep three orders and the historic ordination by bishops, which many Protestant churches do not.
catholic.holy_orders:
In the Catholic Church, Holy Orders is the sacrament by which men are ordained as bishops, priests and deacons, in the ministry which Christ gave to the apostles. A bishop ordains by laying on hands and prayer, and the sacrament imparts a lasting spiritual mark, so that a man remains a priest even if he leaves the active ministry.

A priest is understood to act in the person of Christ, especially when he celebrates the Eucharist and forgives sins in Reconciliation. Only baptized men are ordained, following Christ's choice of the twelve apostles. Many Protestant churches understand ordination as the church's recognition of a person's call and gifts, and set a pastor apart for a task, and often ordain women. A Protestant reader should note that Catholics regard ordination as a sacrament that confers a special grace and character, and not only an appointment.
